rules.quote: Write the name as the organisation writes it
rules.specification: For the definite-article provisions, interpret formal-name uses in emails and letters separately from running body text. Apply the explicit lower-case body-text rule to running prose, including correspondence.
rules.violation_condition: An organisation name has spelling, capitalisation, punctuation, symbols or words that differ from the organisation’s own preferred form, after allowing the stated exceptions.
when: Check the written form of the chosen full or shortened name. Whether a shortened form is established, and whether the full name must be introduced, are separate checks.
For a name written entirely in lower case by the organisation, use an initial capital in body text.
Preserve an initial lower-case letter when the name has a medial capital, including at the beginning of a sentence.
Use the organisation’s preferred capitalisation rather than assuming an all-capital registered business name is its preferred written form.
Preserve the words capitalised in the official name, including on first mention. Generic references are governed by the separate generic-term rule.
In formal-name uses in emails, letters and alphabetical lists, retain an official ‘The’. Do not add it to correspondence names that omit it.
In body text, an article before the name is not necessarily part of the official name; names that omit the article may appear with or without it as the sentence requires.
Include possessive apostrophes only where they form part of the official name.
For a citation to a source published under an earlier organisation name, use the source-name rule rather than requiring the current name.
Later print mentions may omit legal qualifiers such as ‘proprietary’ and ‘limited’ and their shortened forms.
Apply the separate Australian Government full-stop rule to ‘Co’ and ‘Inc’.
rules.why: G-2 keeps official-form cases and exceptions together; G-4 absorbs repeated capitalisation, word-inclusion, article and apostrophe instructions rather than creating overlapping name checks.

tags.violation_condition: A first mention uses only an unexpanded shortened or incomplete name when the full title is required, or expands a name known only by its shortened form.

when: Assess the first mention of the organisation or introduction of its shortened form.
Use the full title on first mention in a publication, including legal-name words or their official shortened forms.
For an organisation known only by its shortened form, retain that form rather than spelling it out, as the IKEA contrast demonstrates.
On subsequent mentions in print documents, words such as ‘proprietary’ and ‘limited’ and their corresponding shortened forms may be omitted.
rules.why: G-2 combines first-mention completeness cases; G-3 records later-print omissions as permission rather than a separate rule.

anchor.quote: Don't add a full stop at the end of ‘Co’ and ‘Inc’ unless they finish a sentence.
anchor.suffix: No full stop is the correct Aus

covers.quote: No full stop is the correct Australian Government style for abbreviations.

examples.note: The abbreviation has no full stop.

parts.quote: Apple Inc

tags.violation_condition: ‘Co’ or ‘Inc’ has a following full stop when the abbreviation does not finish the sentence.

when: ‘Co’ or ‘Inc’ occurs as part of an organisation name.
A sentence-final full stop is allowed.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the sentence-final exception within the abbreviation full-stop check; the explanatory sentence is not a second rule.

tags.violation_condition: A generic reference to an organisation, or a shared generic name referring to several organisations, is capitalised as though it were a proper name.

when: The expression is a generic reference such as ‘the department’ or ‘the agency’, rather than the full official name.
The same lower-case treatment applies when several organisations share the generic name.
An organisation’s own practice of capitalising its generic reference does not override this rule.
rules.why: G-1 leaves the capitalisation grouping heading as a section; G-2 combines individual and collective generic references into one capitalisation check.

anchor.quote: In body text, use lower case for the definite article in the names of organisations

covers.quote: Always use lower case ‘the’ in body text.
covers.suffix: This follows the practice of mo

examples.note: The article is lower case in body text.

parts.quote: Next year the University of Sydney will renovate its science buildings.

tags.specification: Interpret this as a rule about name capitalisation, not ordinary sentence-initial capitals. Apply it to running prose in emails and letters, while preserving official ‘The’ in formal-name uses there. These distinctions resolve wording the page does not expressly reconcile.
tags.violation_condition: A definite article accompanying an organisation name in running body text has an organisational initial capital rather than lower case.

when: The article accompanies an organisation name in running body text, including where the organisation officially capitalises ‘The’.
Under the proposed interpretation, a capital required solely because the article begins a sentence is not a violation.
Formal-name uses in correspondence and alphabetical lists follow the official-name instruction instead.
rules.why: G-4 combines the heading and its emphatic restatement; the proposed interpretation makes the correspondence and sentence-position boundaries explicit.

anchor.quote: arrange by ‘The’ as the first word in the name

tags.violation_condition: An alphabetical list ignores an official initial ‘The’ when ordering an organisation name.

when: The organisation’s official name begins with ‘The’.
The name appears in an alphabetical list.
rules.why: Alphabetical ordering is a distinct property from including or capitalising the article, so it needs its own finding.

anchor.quote: Use the singular verb with organisation names

covers.quote: Always use a singular verb.
This applies even if organisation names end in an ‘s’and look plural.

tags.violation_condition: An organisation name used as a grammatical subject takes a plural verb.

when: The subject denotes an organisation as a single entity.
The rule also applies to organisation names ending in ‘s’ that look plural.
rules.why: G-4 absorbs the body restatement; G-2 keeps plural-looking names as a condition of the same agreement check.
